clue.text: Tea for two — and step lively !

indicators.note: tea for two means the word for tea is served twice over, one helping each

parts.note: cha is an old slang word for tea

explanation.surface: An invitation to a cosy tea for two, followed by a brisk command to get moving.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tea for two' recalls the song, but 'for two' simply doubles CHA, slang for tea; 'and' joins this to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The cha-cha is a lively Latin ballroom dance, so stepping lively describes doing it.

clue.text: Measure of what the Acropolis, for example, may do?

definitions.text: what the Acropolis, for example, may do?

explanation.surface: A question about how much the ancient Acropolis can hold.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as CAP A CITY, the second part is what the Acropolis does, crowning Athens; 'of' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Volume or the amount something holds is a measure; split up, the word says to top a town, as a citadel does Athens.

clue.text: Like Elijah's. exit

parts.note: the prophet Elijah left the earth carried up in a chariot of fire by a whirlwind

explanation.surface: A question about how the prophet left the world.
explanation.walkthrough: In 2 Kings, Elijah is taken up to heaven by a whirlwind, so his departure was through the sky.
explanation.definitionFit: Being carried up through the sky means travelling aloft, as the prophet did in his chariot of fire.

clue.text: Incline to look downtrodden?

explanation.surface: A tendency to appear oppressed.
explanation.walkthrough: A ship heels over when it leans; a shoe trodden down at the back has its heel worn over, so it looks literally downtrodden. 'to' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To lean or tilt sideways, as a boat does; and a well-worn shoe whose heel is bent sideways looks trodden down.

clue.text: Dead Sea fruit cane ?

explanation.surface: A botanical puzzle: what kind of cane grows the fruit of the Dead Sea?
explanation.walkthrough: The Dead Sea fruit, or apple of Sodom, was said to turn to ash in the mouth, so it is a plant of ash; an ash plant is also a walking stick cut from an ash sapling.
explanation.definitionFit: Legend's Dead Sea fruit crumbles to cinders, making it a plant bearing ash; separately, a sapling cut from that tree makes a countryman's walking stick.

clue.text: It's a close thing to calculate the area of a rectangle

definitions.text: calculate the area of a rectangle

explanation.surface: A geometry lesson about working out areas, with a near-miss in it.
explanation.walkthrough: Things side by side are close together; the area of a rectangle is one side multiplied by the adjacent side, read as 'side by side'. 'to' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Placed next to each other means close; multiplying length by width reads as one edge times another.

clue.text: "'Thy is a holy place" (Byron)

parts.note: a line from Byron's Sonnet on Chillon, addressing the castle where Bonivard was held, with one word blanked out

explanation.surface: A quotation from Byron with a word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: Byron's sonnet opens 'Chillon! thy prison is a holy place'; the dash in the printed quotation marks the missing word, and the castle was a jail.
explanation.definitionFit: The Castle of Chillon held the patriot Bonivard captive, so Byron calls its jail sacred ground.

clue.text: If I have to sum up, it is with ill-will

parts.note: an is an archaic word for if, as in Shakespeare's 'an it please you'
taken as written

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the word sum is read from the bottom, so backwards

explanation.surface: A grudging remark that summing up must be done with bad feeling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sum up' looks like a phrase meaning summarise, but 'up' reverses SUM to MUS in this down clue; 'have to' and 'it is with' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: Animus is hostility or animosity, a feeling of enmity towards someone.

clue.text: A canopy for sixpence

explanation.surface: Buying a canopy for sixpence.
explanation.walkthrough: A tester is the canopy over a four-poster bed, and also an old slang name for a sixpence, from the Tudor coin the teston.
explanation.definitionFit: A bed's overhead hanging frame and an old British coin worth half a shilling both share this name.

clue.text: What a come-down for knitwear specialist !

explanation.surface: A sorry fall in fortune for someone who makes jumpers.
explanation.walkthrough: A purler is a heavy headlong fall, and also, as a made-up agent noun, someone who does purl stitches in knitting.
explanation.definitionFit: A heavy headlong tumble is called a purler; one who knits purl stitch would be a purler too.

clue.text: Singular characters these Didoites

indicators.note: singular in the sense of strange or odd tells us the nonsense word is to be oddly rearranged

explanation.surface: These followers of Dido are a peculiar bunch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Didoites' is not a real word but anagram fodder; 'Singular' (meaning strange) signals the rearrangement while also colouring the definition, and 'these' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Eccentric people are called characters or oddities, both meaning unusual individuals.

clue.text: Corot turns to the north for handsome foliage

indicators.note: turns tells us the painter's name is spun round into a new order

parts.note: N is the standard abbreviation for north

explanation.surface: The painter Corot switches to northern scenes to paint fine leaves.
explanation.walkthrough: Corot was a French landscape painter; 'turns' shuffles his name to CROTO, and 'to the north' adds N.
explanation.definitionFit: Croton is a tropical shrub grown as a houseplant for its brightly coloured leaves.

clue.text: Such power brings such corruption

parts.note: a play on Lord Acton's saying that power tends to corrupt and total power corrupts totally

explanation.surface: A political maxim about how power corrupts.
explanation.walkthrough: Lord Acton wrote 'Power tends to corrupt, and absolute power corrupts absolutely'; the one word fills both blanks of 'such'.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective qualifies both the power and the corruption in Lord Acton's famous maxim, meaning total or unrestricted.

clue.text: Violation of rules might be a bit improper in the first place

indicators.note: the first place means the little word in is placed at the front

parts.note: taken as written
a bit is a fraction, and an improper fraction is one whose top is bigger than its bottom

explanation.surface: Breaking the rules might be slightly improper in the first place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in the first place' looks like a filler phrase but puts IN first; 'a bit improper' is a fraction, nodding to an improper fraction. 'might be' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: An infraction is a breach or infringement, as of a law or regulation.

clue.text: Gentle care for a sore nose ?

parts.note: a sore spot is a tender one
a ness is a headland, a nose of land jutting into the sea

explanation.surface: Treating a painful nose with gentle care.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nose' is a headland here, as in place names like Loch Ness's neighbour Sheerness; 'for' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Gentle, loving care for someone is called tenderness, the quality of being soft and kind.

clue.text: Prickly from the hot season abroad, round China

indicators.note: round means the summer word goes around the country's name

parts.note: ete is the French word for summer, the hot season in France
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone irritable after a summer spent travelling around China.
explanation.walkthrough: 'abroad' points to French: ETE (été) is summer; 'from' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Echinate is a botanical term meaning covered with spines, like a hedgehog or sea urchin.

clue.text: Define exact position and be sharp about it

explanation.surface: Advice to locate something precisely and quickly.
explanation.walkthrough: To pinpoint is to locate exactly; the point of a pin is literally sharp.
explanation.definitionFit: To locate something precisely is to pinpoint it; a pin's tip is the sharpest of ends.

clue.text: Batsman's tragedy at The Eagle

explanation.surface: A cricketer's sad dismissal at a pub called The Eagle.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a batsman out at once has gone in and out; the nursery rhyme 'Pop Goes the Weasel' goes 'Up and down the City Road, in and out the Eagle', a London pub.
explanation.definitionFit: A batter dismissed almost immediately is in and out; the old rhyme about the City Road has people going to and fro at the Eagle tavern.

clue.text: Foreword ?

parts.note: read as fore-word, a word spoken beforehand about what is to come

explanation.surface: A book's preface.
explanation.walkthrough: A foreword is normally a preface, but split as 'fore-word' it is a word about the future spoken in advance.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying what will happen before it does is a forecast, a statement made ahead of events.

clue.text: Engraved like the pot of a pot-hunter?

definitions.text: like the pot of a pot-hunter?

explanation.surface: Describing a decorated trophy won by a prize-chaser.
explanation.walkthrough: Chased metal is engraved or embossed; a pot-hunter chases pots, sporting trophies, so the cup was literally pursued.
explanation.definitionFit: Silver decorated by tooling is called chased; a trophy-seeker's cup was pursued before it was won.

clue.text: "The call of incense breathing morn " (Gray)

definitions.text: The call of incense breathing morn

parts.words: The call of incense breathing morn
parts.note: a line from Gray's Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard with one adjective blanked out

explanation.surface: A line of Gray's poetry with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Gray's Elegy reads 'The breezy call of incense-breathing Morn'; the dash in the printed quotation marks the missing word.
explanation.definitionFit: Gray describes the dawn's summons as airy and fresh, like a light wind.

clue.text: What's the grievance at home in the flat?

indicators.note: in tells us the words for at home are placed inside the word for the flat

parts.note: a plat is a flat plot of ground
in means at home, as in staying in

explanation.surface: A question about what complaint is being aired at home in a flat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flat' looks like an apartment but is PLAT, a flat patch of land; 'What's the' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A plaint is a complaint or lament, an expression of grievance.

clue.text: Sympathy for one struck by a horseshoe ?

definitions.text: for one struck by a horseshoe ?

explanation.surface: Consoling someone hit by a supposedly lucky horseshoe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hard luck!' is a phrase of sympathy; a horseshoe is a lucky charm, so being struck by one is luck that is literally hard.
explanation.definitionFit: The exclamation offers commiseration; literally, a lucky charm made of iron that hits you is fortune of the solid kind.

clue.text: Philip reaching the green flag, gets an apple

parts.note: Pip is a pet name for Philip, as with Pip in Great Expectations
on a golf green the flag marking the hole is called the pin

explanation.surface: A golfer named Philip reaches the flag on the green and is rewarded with an apple.
explanation.walkthrough: 'green' is the golf green, not a colour; 'reaching' and 'gets' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: A pippin is a variety of eating apple, such as Cox's Orange Pippin.

clue.text: The remedy is precise.

explanation.surface: A statement that the cure is exact.
explanation.walkthrough: As a noun a specific is a medicine for one particular disease; as an adjective it means precise.
explanation.definitionFit: A drug targeting one particular disease was called a specific; the adjective means exact or definite.

clue.text: Show me the, fun-place so I can change

indicators.note: change tells us the words so I can are to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A request to be shown the place of fun so the speaker can get changed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Show me the' is a link leading to the definition; 'change' rearranges the letters of 'so I can'.
explanation.definitionFit: A gambling house with roulette and card tables is a place of entertainment, so a fun-place.

clue.text: Within these walls, mortar-boards are unnecessary

definitions.text: Within these walls, mortar-boards are unnecessary

parts.words: Within these walls, mortar-boards are unnecessary
parts.note: the academic caps called mortar-boards suggest a college, but read literally they are boards holding builders' mortar, needless for walls built without it

explanation.surface: An institution where academic caps need not be worn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Within these walls' sounds like a school, and mortar-boards are graduation caps; but a builder's mortar-board holds mortar, and a dry-stone wall is built without any.
explanation.definitionFit: Field walls of stacked stones with no mortar binding them are a traditional rural building method.

clue.text: Formed from two sets (of-three each?)

indicators.note: formed from says the letters are reshaped out of the material that follows

parts.note: the word sets taken literally twice gives two copies of the letters of set
the word sets taken literally twice gives two copies of the letters of set

explanation.surface: Something made up of two groups, perhaps three apiece.
explanation.walkthrough: Two copies of SET rearranged give the answer, and the whole clue defines it: the six lines of a sonnet's close are often two groups of three.
explanation.definitionFit: A six-line stanza or closing section of a Petrarchan sonnet, often rhymed as two tercets.
